opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's an interesting one, because on the surface you'd think search makes it easy. Pokémon is one of the most documented games on the internet. There are walkthroughs, wikis, Reddit threads, speedrun guides. The answer to "where do I go next" is almost always out there. So the hard part isn't really finding information.

The hard part is grounding it. A walkthrough says something like "head north out of Cerulean, cross the bridge, beat the trainers," and the model has to map that onto what's actually on its screen right now: a grid of pixels, its current position, a menu that might be open, an NPC blocking the path. That translation from text knowledge to the state of the game is where things break down. The model can know exactly what to do in the abstract and still walk into the same wall fifty times.

There's also a state-tracking problem. Guides assume you're on the canonical path. If the model has done things out of order, or its party is underleveled, or it missed an item, the guide is subtly wrong for its situation, and the model has to notice that and adapt rather than following the instructions blindly. That needs a robust internal sense of "where am I in this game," and long-horizon memory is still pretty weak in these agent setups.

And then there's a meta question about what you're even measuring. If the model can search for everything, you're testing retrieval plus execution, not reasoning or exploration. Part of what makes Pokémon a cool benchmark is seeing whether a model can figure things out the way a kid would, by poking around, trying things, building a mental model of the world. Search shortcuts some of that. So deciding when to search versus when to just reason it out is itself a hard problem, and arguably the most interesting one.

So to me, search solves the knowledge bottleneck, but it exposes the real bottlenecks, which are perception, planning over long horizons, and knowing how to use outside information instead of just having it.

r001.rationale: The response says the hard part is grounding walkthrough knowledge in the game’s current visual state, including the player’s position, open menus, and obstacles.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think people assume the hard part is retrieval, like can the model find the right page on Bulbapedia. That's actually the easy part. The hard part is grounding. Pokémon is this really long-horizon, partially observable thing, and the model's problem is almost never "I don't know what Rock Tunnel is." It's "I don't know where I am right now, and I don't know how what I just read maps onto the pixels in front of me."

So you search, you get back a walkthrough that says "go north from the Pokémon Center and talk to the guy by the ledge," and that's written for a human who already has a persistent mental model of the map. The model doesn't have that. Every step it's re-deriving state from a screenshot, and the search result is kind of this disembodied text that it has to stitch onto a very noisy, very local view of the world. That stitching is where things fall apart. You see models confidently following instructions for a room they're not in.

The second thing, which I think is underrated, is that search makes the model worse at knowing when to stop. Without search, if the model is stuck, it'll eventually just try things, bump into walls, and sometimes that random exploration actually works. With search, there's this attractor where it goes "let me look that up," gets a plausible-sounding answer, acts on it, it doesn't work, and then it searches again with a slightly different query. You get these loops that look very productive in the transcript and are totally non-productive in the game. So the agentic question is really about calibration, like when is external information actually going to resolve my uncertainty versus when is my uncertainty about my own state, where no amount of searching helps.

And then there's the boring but real stuff. Walkthroughs are for a specific version, so you get Red versus Yellow versus some romhack, and the model has no way to validate which one applies. Context length matters too. If you're dumping search results into context every few steps across tens of thousands of actions, you're mostly just polluting the model's memory of what it actually did. So you end up needing some kind of summarization or scratchpad layer anyway, and at that point the interesting research is in the memory, not in the search.

r001.rationale: It says retrieval is easy and identifies grounding as the hard part: the model must connect walkthrough text to its current location and the pixels in the game.

astra-6.text: I think the hard part is knowing what to search for and then grounding that information in the game state. You can find a walkthrough that tells you where to go, but the model still has to figure out, “Where am I? Have I already done that step? What’s preventing me from moving forward?” And then it has to translate that into actions. So finding the information is only part of it. The harder part is closing that loop: search, act, observe what changed, and decide whether the advice actually helped.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the model must ground walkthrough information in the game state, determine where it is and what has changed, and translate that into actions. This clearly identifies applying web-derived knowledge to Pokémon’s game state as the hard part.

sol-6.1.text: I think the hard part is knowing what to search for and then grounding that information in the current game state. You can look up a walkthrough, but the walkthrough assumes you know where you are, what you’ve already done, and which prerequisites you’ve satisfied. The model has to connect that high-level advice to the actions it can actually take. So retrieving the information is only one piece. Maintaining the state and figuring out whether that information applies right now is the harder part.

r001.rationale: The response says the model must ground web information in the current game state and connect advice to possible actions, but it does not identify Pokémon’s visual game state as the context.
